mappings.note: Identifying a thermoplastic from its linear monomer arrangement and typical products is classification from given properties. Duplicate of an earlier item and coded the same way.
Rayon resembling silk is the natural-versus-human-made fibre comparison LO-1 names. Not LO-2, which is used here for plastic classes.
Naming the polymer that coats cookware and iron soles applies material properties to household objects. Not LO-1, since the use rather than the contrast is the point.
Picking the poor conductor differentiates materials by an electrical property, which LO-1 names with conductors and insulators. Not LO-2, because no metal/non-metal class is assigned.
PVC for water pipes is choosing the right material for an everyday job. Not LO-2, because no polymer class is being judged.
Finding the substance that is liquid at room temperature sorts materials by a physical property. Not LO-2, since no metal/non-metal grouping is required.
Ranking metals to find the most reactive compares them on a chemical property. Not LO-6, which is used here for items about what a reaction actually produces.
Mercury as the liquid metal is a property-based identification. Not LO-2, because the item does not ask whether it is a metal.
The most ductile metal compares materials on a physical property. Not LO-12, since no application follows from it here.
Sodium as the most reactive metal is a property comparison. Deliberately different from the storage item below, which asks what to keep it in and is therefore an application.

The gas from magnesium and dilute hydrochloric acid is the product side of a metal-acid reaction, the content of LO-6's word equations. Not LO-1, because a reaction product rather than a property is asked for.
The metal that resists air, water and acid is identified by its inertness, a property. Not LO-6, which covers what a reaction yields rather than which metal avoids reacting.
The general properties of metals are exactly the differentiation of materials by property. Not LO-2, because no material is being sorted into a class.
Naming metalloids as the in-between class is classification of materials, the metals/non-metals example in the outcome. Not LO-1, because a class is named rather than two materials contrasted.
Which metal reacts readily with cold water is metal-water reaction knowledge, LO-6's territory. Not LO-1, which covers physical properties rather than reaction behaviour.
The best electrical conductor ranks materials by conductivity. Not LO-12, because no device or use is chosen.
Galvanising iron with zinc applies material science to protect an everyday object. Not LO-6, because the item names the coating rather than the reaction.
Comparing which metal reacts more with water is reaction behaviour with water, LO-6's subject. Not LO-1, reserved here for physical properties.
Placing boron in the metalloid class is classification of an element by its characteristics. Not LO-1, because no property comparison is drawn.
Defining an ore as the mineral worth extracting from classifies minerals by a characteristic. Not LO-12, because no extraction is carried out.
Which metals catch fire in air is a reaction-with-air question, named in LO-6. Not LO-1, because the item is about reactivity rather than a physical property.
Magnesium oxide dissolving to give a basic solution is the product character of a metal-oxide reaction with water. Not LO-2, because no material is being classified.
The metal that does not react even with steam is reaction-with-water knowledge. Not LO-1, which covers inertness as a property only where no reagent is named.
Bromine as the liquid non-metal is a physical-property identification. Not LO-2, because the item already tells the pupil it is a non-metal.
Tin rather than zinc on food cans is choosing an appropriate metal, named verbatim in LO-12. Not LO-6, because the reaction is the reason rather than the question.
Metals forming basic oxides with oxygen is the product character of a metal-air reaction. Not LO-2, since oxides are not being sorted into classes here but produced.
Sulphur giving an acidic oxide is the non-metal counterpart of the same reaction-with-air outcome. Kept on LO-6 for the same reason as the metal-oxide item.
Zinc and aluminium with sodium hydroxide releasing hydrogen is a reaction product question. Not LO-1, because no property is compared.
Naming malleability as the beating-into-sheets property is differentiation of materials by property. Not LO-2, because no substance is being classified.
Naming ductility as the drawing-into-wires property is the same property-naming task. Not LO-12, since no use is chosen.
Picking which substance can be beaten into sheets amounts to sorting metals from non-metals, LO-2's own example. Not LO-1, which fits the items that name the property instead of applying it to sort.
Defining sonorousness as ringing when struck is a property definition. Not LO-2, because no element is being classified.
Picking the odd element out of a set turns on the metal/non-metal classification the outcome names. Not LO-1, because no single property is compared across all four.
Lustre as the shine property of metals is property naming. Not LO-2, since no material is sorted.
A lustrous non-metal is the exception that tests the metal/non-metal classification. Not LO-1, because the pupil must place the substance in a class despite the property.
Storing sodium under kerosene is a safe-handling practice applied in the laboratory and daily life. Kept apart from the item asking which metal is most reactive, which is a property comparison.
Malleability named again as the sheet-forming property; property naming is LO-1. Duplicate of an earlier item and coded the same way.
Picking the metal from a list is the metals/non-metals classification verbatim. Not LO-1, because no property is being compared.
Picking the non-metal is the mirror of the previous item and the same classification outcome. Not LO-1, for the same reason.
